The post Applicants still believe in university – but their expectations are changing   appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
HEPI is recruiting our first Communications Manager. In this exciting role, you will help shape how we share our research, events and ideas. Visit this webpage for the full job description and details of how to apply. Deadline 26th July.

This blog was kindly authored by Simon Jones, Group Higher Education Director at Unite Students. Unite Students is a HEPI Partner.

Now in its fifth year, Unite Student’s Applicant Index provides a unique view of how attitudes towards university are evolving. This year, 2,200 university applicants were surveyed on topics including support services, finance and the perceived value of higher education. Applicants continue to believe in the value of higher education, but they are arriving with increasingly complex expectations and pressures.

For universities, the challenge has long extended beyond simply attracting students. The latest findings suggest that applicants are balancing study with work, wellbeing concerns and future career ambitions earlier than ever before.

Working while studying: a new normal

One of the most striking findings from this year’s report is how deeply embedded paid work has become in student life. Having a job during term time is now the norm. An overwhelming 87% of applicants expect to work during term time, with nearly a third planning to take on more than 16 hours a week.

Whilst part of this will undoubtably be due to a financial necessity – the maximum maintenance loan available to English students covers only 50% of their costs – there is more to the story. Today’s applicants increasingly view employment as part of the university experience itself: an opportunity to develop skills, gain experience and build confidence for future careers alongside their studies. Work is becoming a key part of how students prepare for life after graduation.

For universities, this challenges traditional assumptions about student engagement. Paid work is no longer simply a supplementary activity, but now is an everyday part of student life. Institutions may therefore need to consider how academic delivery, support services and careers provision reflect the realities of a cohort balancing multiple demands on their time.

At the same time, the findings raise important questions about balance. Juggling academic commitments with significant working hours can place pressure on time, energy and wellbeing. Supporting students to manage these competing priorities will become increasingly important.

The university experience still holds strong appeal

Despite the increasing financial pressures, it’s clear that the overall university experience still holds value, with most applicants intending to move away from home. This demonstrates a continued desire for independence and immersion in a new environment.

Applicants continue to prioritise opportunities to grow personally and build social connections. University is still seen as a transformative experience which transcends lectures and exams.

Wellbeing, welcome and belonging paint a more complex picture

Encouragingly, 74% of applicants expect to feel welcome, and 65% anticipate a sense of belonging at university. These figures reflect a positive outlook and strong expectations of inclusive, supportive communities.

Yet there are signs of fragility. Confidence has dropped slightly in several key areas that directly influence student success, particularly wellbeing, resilience and future employment prospects.

While applicants clearly remain hopeful, they’re aware of the challenges ahead. The combination of academic pressure, financial demands and the need to balance work and study may be factors cultivating a more cautious outlook.

Strengthening the building blocks of student experience

Social confidence has fallen, with around 26% of applicants stating they feel lonely all or most of the time, with fewer saying they have someone to turn to in a crisis. These results are compounded for care-experienced, estranged, LGBTQ+, disabled and neurodivergent students, who all report lower confidence, higher loneliness and greater need for support.

Across the five years of the Applicant Index, these equity gaps have remained persistent, underlining the importance of inclusive environments that help residents settle, connect and feel part of a wider community.

Shaping the future of student experience

Students believe in the value of university and want the full experience, but they need to belong to institutions that recognise and respond to this reality by creating environments where students can succeed, both during their studies and beyond.

This means:

Providing flexible learning options that accommodate working students

Strengthening wellbeing and mental health support

Creating opportunities for belonging and community-building

Helping students connect their work experiences to long-term career goals

Overall, the 2026 cohort remains motivated by the opportunities higher education offers, including living and learning independently. While pressures remain, the central story is one of sustained demand and enduring belief in the value of university.

title: Fumbling Toward an AI Policy
summary:
Fumbling Toward an AI Policy
Sara Brady Fri, 07/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

You can pry my em dashes from my cold, dead hands.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
I’ve seen a common theme among faculty posting about AI: “We’re out on our own here! Why won’t the administration set a clear policy?”

In the abstract, it seems like a compelling question. But getting from “we need a policy” to “we need this policy” is much harder than it sounds.

Part of that is because AI is a rapidly moving target. In just a few years, it has gone from a lab model to a seemingly mandatory future, even as it functions on the ground as a paper-o-matic. It’s moving much more quickly than the policy-development process can, making it likely that any policy would be obsolete by the time it’s enacted. Yet it’s everywhere; just last weekend, my younger niece, who is halfway through high school, informed me confidently that “everyone uses it.”

Some employers seem to want AI fluency, though they don’t seem to know quite what that means, and now some firms are desperate enough for students who haven’t outsourced their thinking that they’re hiring humanities majors and training them on tech. It’s a return to a much older model—and, frankly, a welcome one.

A policy of a Great Refusal would hold real appeal to instructors who are (rightly!) tired of reading slop passed off as actual student work. But it would put students at a possible competitive disadvantage when they’re up against others who have done compelling work with it. It also presumes that AI can only be used for bad ends. Given how quickly it’s evolving, I’d be reluctant to declare that it could only ever do harm, even as I see tremendous harm currently being done. That would effectively preclude innovation. (I’ve heard of instructors having students proofread slop as an editing exercise; there’s something to that.) And it would force instructors to enforce rules that are so widely ignored as to call the legitimacy of enforcement into question. When culture and rules grow too far apart, culture wins.

The environmental objection to AI is real at this point, though I don’t know if it always will be. I could imagine data centers becoming much more efficient over time, at which point the environmental objection would be obsolete. If the real objection is to slop, then object to slop.

(Personally, I object to AI’s co-optation of the em dash. The em dash is a perfectly honorable writing tool. As Elle Cordova memorably put it, just because it got caught in ChatGPT’s teeth doesn’t make it bad.)

A Great Refusal would create serious issues in computer science classes and, increasingly, in allied health programs. As it becomes part of the practice of fields for which we’re preparing students, leaving it out would leave a gap in their preparation. It could even put ethics classes in a tough spot, since students would be asked to pass judgment on something they couldn’t try themselves.

A policy of “you can use it for suggestions and structure, but not for content” is likely much too nuanced and subtle to be enforceable.

A policy of laissez-faire is effectively no policy at all.

A policy of “it’s the future, so we encourage students to use it” effectively surrenders to the paper-o-matic. An old joke compares artificial intelligence to natural stupidity; my concern is that the former leaves the latter undisturbed. The point of writing, say, a five-page paper analyzing a marketing campaign, social movement or novel is not the paper itself; it’s the process of creating the paper. That’s where the learning happens. If the process is reduced to a prompt, that’s where the learning stops. It’s the difference between running a marathon and driving one. Yes, driving one is faster, but it doesn’t get you into shape. Letting marathoners drive cars defeats the purpose of a marathon.

A policy of letting each academic department set its own policy has the advantage of potentially distinguishing computer programming classes from sociology classes. But it also leads to incoherence on the ground, and a potential race to the bottom as departments compete for enrollments. And for very small departments, it’s not much different from no policy at all.

All of these assume that what AI looks like won’t change meaningfully for years. Given what we’ve seen over the last few years, that’s a bad bet.

Right now, plenty of institutions are taking the view that it’s better to wait for the dust to settle before making sweeping declarations. To someone exasperated by the paper-o-matic, I can understand why that might look like capitulation. But filling in the blanks of an actual policy—when it’s ubiquitous on the ground and the mechanisms are changing we speak—is somewhere between aspirational and hubristic. And even as I say that, I join the refusers in declaring that you can pry my em dashes from my cold, dead hands.

title: Harvard President Discusses Federal Fight
summary:
Harvard President Discusses Federal Fight
Josh Moody Fri, 07/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

Alan Garber talked about the university’s legal fight with the federal government—and its implications for higher ed and the nation—in an interview at an event in D.C. Thursday.

Byline(s)
Josh Moody
full_text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Alan Garber’s lawyer told him he shouldn’t speak at the Economic Club on Thursday, in the midst of his institution’s protracted legal battle with the Trump administration over federal research funding.

The Harvard University president did so anyway, spending almost an hour in a friendly interview with David Rubenstein, a Harvard donor and co-founder of the private equity firm the Carlyle Group. Throughout the interview, Garber argued that Harvard’s legal battle with the federal government—which has sought to cut off $2.2 billion in research funding over allegations that the university mishandled antisemitism on campus—could have far-reaching consequences not only for Harvard and the higher education sector but also the nation.

Though Harvard won the first round in its legal battle last fall when a federal judge determined that the funding freeze was illegal, a Trump administration appeal is still playing out. The Department of Justice also sued Harvard in February, alleging the university was slow-walking responses to an investigation into its admissions processes. (Harvard has denied the claims in the DOJ lawsuit.)

Multiple congressional investigations into Harvard are also in motion.

“Many universities have settled with the Trump administration on various points the Trump administration has made against them. Harvard has famously not settled,” said Rubenstein, who at times appeared more an ally than an inquisitor, prompting applause. “How come you haven’t settled, and are you planning to look for a settlement?”

Garber quickly noted, “There are some things I can’t say.” Then he offered a response that largely sidestepped the settlement question but underscored the stakes of the legal fight.

“This is about the relationship between the federal government and America’s universities, and that’s particularly true for America’s research universities,” he said. “Research funding has been withheld in order to force agreements about some issues that—for us and for other universities—cross red lines having to do with the ability of universities to use their judgment in deciding what kind of research to perform, which students they should admit, which faculty should be hired, what we teach and so on.”

Garber added that while research universities and the federal government have long had a strong relationship, the fight threatens to imperil the nation’s standing in science and technology, which raises concerns not just for higher education but also for the national interest.

He later noted that while universities are pursuing philanthropy, corporate partnerships and cost reductions to mitigate the impact of the funding cuts, ultimately “nobody can replace the federal government.”

Rubenstein also asked about the exodus of scientists and other researchers to countries such as China, though Garber noted that is not an issue for Harvard. He said he was more concerned about the declining inflow of talent due to restrictions on international students, including the recently proposed effort to limit the amount of time they can study in the U.S.

But even as international enrollments slip across the country, Garber said, the numbers have held strong for Harvard, though the university has seen shifts. Some schools on campus have welcomed fewer international students, he said, while others have seen stronger numbers.

Rubenstein also asked him how Harvard has taken the fight to Capitol Hill through lobbying efforts. To date, Garber said, he’s met with an estimated 160 members of Congress. While some have been “hostile,” he said he’s had more good than bad meetings with lawmakers.

“Congress has an important role to play in basically defending research,” Garber said. “That is where there are members of both parties who very much believe in the importance of the American research enterprise. And yes, we are visiting Congress. Yes, we are making the case, and it is having an effect. But in some cases, it’s not very hard to persuade people because they see what’s at stake and they recognize more of that privately than they sometimes do publicly.”

An Inside Higher Ed analysis found that Harvard spent $950,000 on federal lobbying efforts in 2025. So far, Harvard has spent $430,000 this year, according to federal lobbying disclosures.

Rubenstein also jokingly asked Garber about the job itself and whether he would wish it on a friend or enemy. In response, Garber said it was a bit like being a beekeeper: Ultimately, it’s not so bad as long as you’re not allergic to being stung.

title: On Keeping Sanity and Purpose While Higher Ed and DEI Are Under Attack
summary:
On Keeping Sanity and Purpose While Higher Ed and DEI Are Under Attack
Elizabeth Redden Fri, 07/24/2026 - 03:00 AM

I offer four considerations to help navigate the year ahead.

Byline(s)
Cameron C. Beatty
full_text:
Summer break is supposed to be a time to rest, recover and remember that we are human beings before we are faculty members, administrators, advisers, committee chairs, emergency responders, unofficial therapists, budget translators and professional email archaeologists. And yet, even in summer, higher education has a way of following us.

I tried to use this summer to breathe. To step away. To recover some sense of balance after another academic year of shifting policies, nervous institutional language, political attacks and the familiar exhaustion of doing equity work in institutions that often celebrate the idea of justice more comfortably than the practice of it. I wanted to return to the next academic year with renewed clarity, a little more rest and maybe fewer tabs open in my brain.

Then, on the 250th anniversary of this country’s founding, white supremacists marched in our nation’s capital. That image is hard to shake. As the country commemorated its founding promises of liberty, freedom and democracy, organized symbols of hate showed up in public view. And for those of us who work in higher education, the meaning of that moment should not be abstract. The people participating in those marches could be our students. They could be our students’ parents. They could be donors, trustees, elected officials, community partners or, if we are honest, maybe even our colleagues. That is not a comfortable sentence to write. But comfort has never been a reliable measure of truth.

This moment makes clearer why diversity, equity and inclusion education is not optional, ornamental or outdated. DEI is not a slogan. It is not a branding exercise. It is not a campus accessory to pull out during heritage months and quietly hide when the political weather changes. At its best, DEI education helps people understand history, power, identity, inequality, institutional responsibility and democratic life. It helps us name harm before harm becomes normalized. It helps students and communities develop the tools to recognize propaganda, resist dehumanization and build more just relationships with one another.

White supremacist extremism does not emerge from nowhere. It is taught, absorbed, circulated, legitimized, excused and sometimes protected by silence. If higher education cannot help students critically examine racism, antisemitism, nationalism, gendered violence, homophobia, transphobia, xenophobia and other forms of organized hate, then we have misunderstood our educational mission.

And still, in too many places, the response to this moment has been institutional shrinking. The language changes. The policies shift. The emails get vaguer. The meetings get longer. Programs are renamed. Statements are softened. Trainings are paused. People are told to be “careful,” though careful often seems to mean quiet.

Recent courtroom developments remind us that institutional timidity is not always based on firm legal foundations. In early July, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit upheld the injunction against the higher education provisions of Florida’s Stop WOKE Act (HB 7), reaffirming that the state where I teach cannot dictate which viewpoints faculty may express in university classrooms. Yet even as parts of HB 7 have been blocked in Florida, the broader wave of anti-DEI legislation has already reshaped institutional behavior at colleges across the country. Campuses have renamed programs, removed language, canceled initiatives and embraced a culture of overcompliance that often extends well beyond what the law requires.

Those of us whose work is rooted in equity, inclusion, justice, belonging, access and student thriving are living through a deeply complicated moment. For many of us, this is not simply professional work. It is personal, intellectual, ethical and spiritual work. We entered higher education because we believed colleges and universities could be places of transformation. We believed students deserved more than credentials. They deserved care, challenge, truth, community and the opportunity to imagine themselves into futures that systems were not always built to support.

So when diversity, equity and inclusion work is targeted, diluted, renamed, erased or quietly pushed into the shadows, it can feel like more than a policy shift. It can feel like an attack on the very reason many of us came into this profession in the first place.

And still, I am trying to hold on to both my sanity and my purpose.

That does not mean pretending everything is fine. Sometimes keeping your sanity means admitting, plainly, “This is absurd.” Sometimes it means closing the laptop before sending an email that probably should have stayed in drafts. Sometimes it means finding the colleague who can understand your facial expression on Zoom before you even unmute.

But sanity also requires remembering that the current moment, while exhausting, is not the whole story. Higher education has always been a contested terrain. Access has always been fought for. Inclusion has always been resisted. The classroom, the committee meeting, the advising session, the research project, the student organization and the mentoring conversation all remain sites where possibility can still be practiced.

The work of scholars such as Sara Ahmed, Shaun Harper and Lori Patton Davis helps us understand why this moment matters. Ahmed’s research on institutional complaint illustrates how universities often frame complaints about racism or exclusion as organizational problems to be managed rather than injustices to be addressed. Harper’s scholarship on racial equity and campus racial climates pushes higher education to move beyond symbolic commitments and toward measurable institutional responsibility. Patton Davis’s work on Black women, race, higher education and critical approaches to student development reminds us that equity work must be historically grounded, intersectional and attentive to those most often pushed to the margins of institutional life.

Together, their work reminds us that institutions do not become equitable because they say the right words. They become more equitable when people are willing to examine power, tell the truth, repair harm and change practice.

As we enter the next academic year, especially for those of us whose work embodies DEI even when the acronym itself is treated like contraband, I offer four considerations informed by the work of Ahmed, Harper and Patton Davis.

First, question and challenge institutional overcompliance.

One of the most frustrating parts of this moment is not only the existence of restrictive policies, but the way some institutions respond to them. Too often, decisions to cut or rename trainings, committees or programs are made in the name of compliance without a clear explanation of what law, policy, regulation or formal guidance actually requires the change. And when people ask why, the answer is often a foggy combination of “legal concerns,” “the current climate” or “we were advised.” That is not enough.

Those of us in higher education should ask careful and direct questions, with an eye toward documentation: What specific policy requires this decision? Who made this interpretation? Is this a legal requirement or an institutional choice? What values are guiding the response? What are the consequences for students, staff and faculty who relied on this work?

Questioning overcompliance is not about being reckless. It is about insisting that fear should not become policy by another name. Institutions should not abandon commitments without explanation. And they certainly should not ask the people most invested in equity to quietly absorb the consequences of decisions that no one is willing to fully own.

We also cannot be cowards in the face of gaslighting about what DEI means. DEI is being misrepresented as exclusion, indoctrination or preferential treatment when, in practice, it often involves the most basic commitments to fairness, access, historical accuracy, inclusive learning and institutional accountability. We should not allow bad-faith definitions to become the operating language of our institutions.

Second, tell the truth about why this work is necessary.

The presence of white supremacist extremism in public life is not separate from higher education. It is connected to what people learn, what they do not learn, what they are taught to fear and what they are permitted to misunderstand. When individuals can march under symbols of hate while claiming patriotism, we are witnessing a failure of civic education, historical memory and moral imagination.

DEI education helps students understand that democracy is not sustained by celebration alone. It requires knowledge, responsibility and the ability to live with people across differences without dehumanizing them. It asks us to examine whose freedom has been protected, whose has been delayed and whose has been actively denied.

That work is not divisive. Racism is divisive. White supremacy is divisive. Historical erasure is divisive. DEI education, when done well, gives us tools to confront those divisions honestly rather than pretending they do not exist.

Third, protect your purpose from institutional mood swings.

Institutions can be fickle. One year, they celebrate equity work in glossy reports and strategic plans. The next year, they act like the same work wandered onto campus without a visitor’s pass.

If your sense of purpose is tied only to institutional affirmation, this moment will drain you quickly. The work must be grounded in something deeper than whether the university is currently comfortable saying the words out loud. That does not mean ignoring institutional realities. We have to be strategic. We have to be attentive to language, policy and risk. But we also have to remember that the purpose of our work did not originate in a branding campaign, and it does not disappear because a web page changed.

Students still need mentors. Faculty and staff still need communities of support. Curricula still need to tell the truth. Research still needs to illuminate inequity and imagine something better. Belonging still matters. Justice still matters. Access still matters. The institution may change its vocabulary. We do not have to surrender our values.

Fourth, build community and practice sustainable courage.

This is not the year to be heroic and isolated. Lone-wolf equity work may sound noble, but in practice it often leads to burnout, resentment and unnecessary vulnerability. We need people who can think with us, strategize with us, laugh with us, pray with us, vent with us and remind us who we are when the work gets heavy.

Courage is not always loud. Sometimes courage is asking the question in the meeting that everyone else is thinking. Sometimes it is documenting a decision. Sometimes it is mentoring a student who feels abandoned by the institution. Sometimes it is publishing the article, teaching the text, preserving the program or refusing to let coded language go uninterrogated.

But courage also has to be sustainable. We cannot confuse constant availability with commitment. We cannot let institutions extract our labor, our health and our joy in the name of mission. Rest is not a betrayal of the work. Boundaries are not evidence that we care less. They are part of how we remain able to care at all.

This next academic year will require discernment. There will be moments to push, moments to pause, moments to document, moments to gather and moments to simply breathe. Not every battle will be ours to fight in the same way. But we can still move with clarity.

I remain hopeful, not because I am naïve about what higher education is facing, but because I have seen what committed people can do even in constrained conditions. I have seen students find language for their experiences. I have seen faculty and staff create spaces of care when official structures failed. I have seen people refuse erasure, even when refusal had to be quiet, creative and strategic.

The attacks are real. The exhaustion is real. The uncertainty is real. The extremism is real. But so is the purpose.

And for those of us who believe higher education should be more honest, more just, more humane and more accountable, the work continues. Maybe with fewer acronyms. Maybe with more receipts. Maybe with a stronger group chat. But it continues.

title: US to top universities: Scientists can 'help' America beat China more than you
summary: The US government plans to fund individual scientists directly, moving away from large institutions. This strategic shift aims to accelerate technological discovery and maintain American leadership in science. Federal agencies are tasked with submitting action plans within ninety days for implementation. The report emphasizes revitalizing science and technology through AI and new research organizations. This initiative seeks to ensure scientific advancements benefit all Americans across the nation.
full_text:
The US government plans to give money to individual scientists directly, instead of large universities and established institutions like Harvard, Stanford and MIT for science and research, especially in the AI era. The Trump administration has sent a memo to federal departments and agencies, outlining the roadmap to revitalize American research and development (R&D). According to a White House press release, the overhaul plan was laid out in a report titled ‘Science: A New Golden Age’ published by Assistant to the President and Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) Michael Kratsios. The directives will help shape a roughly $200 billion annual federal research and development budget across the government for the rest of President Donald Trump’s second term. In both report and memo, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy argues that individual scientists can accelerate technological discovery to defeat China. “American scientific progress was the beating heart of the 20th century. After World War II, we adapted to a new world by reinventing our scientific institutions, and we must do so again today. This report lays a policy foundation that frees American scientists to do their most groundbreaking work, revives the national pursuit of ambitious scientific missions, and positions the United States to lead the AI-driven scientific revolution that will define the next century,” said Director Kratsios.

What this may mean for Harvard, Stanford, MIT and other US universities

The Trump administration said it wants to give more support to programs that fund individual researchers instead of colleges and universities. The report further points to programs such as the National Science Foundation's graduate fellowships and the National Institutes of Health's awards for innovative scientists as examples to follow. It also says that some universities could face challenges under a proposed Office of Management and Budget rule. The proposal would give political appointees more control over research grants and make sure funding matches the administration's priorities. As per a Wall Street Journal report, the new guidance may hurt large universities that rely on federal research funding. The White House has given federal R&D agencies “to submit an action plan within 90 days outlining implementation of these priority practices, while incorporating the budget guidance into their FY2028 submissions to the Office of Management and Budget”.

4 key recommendations made in the federal report

The report organizes its recommendations to government, industry, academia, and philanthropy around four key pillars:

Revitalize America’s Science and Technology Enterprise

The R&D enterprise should refocus support on individual scientists rather than legacy institutions, diversify funding mechanisms beyond slow consensus peer review, create agile new research organizations such as X-Labs and expanded ARPA-like entities, and establish metascience units to institutionalize continuous improvement.

Secure U.S. Dominance in Critical and Emerging Technologies

Federal R&D should prioritize national mission-driven scientific initiatives that unite government, industry, academia, and philanthropy around ambitious goals. These include the Genesis Mission to double the productivity of American research through AI; the Quantum Computer for Application Development and Discovery Science (QC-ADDS); commercial fusion power demonstration by the mid-2030s; crewed lunar return and lunar base development; and next-generation semiconductor technologies.

Launch a New Golden Age Powered by AI for Science

The Federal government should fully fund and scale the Genesis Mission as the flagship national AI-for-science initiative to dramatically accelerate discovery; develop domain-specific scientific foundation models and high-value datasets, invest in AI-enabled verification infrastructure and autonomous laboratories; and begin transitioning toward AI-native scientific institutions better suited to an era of machine-augmented research.

Ensure That Science and Technology Better the Lives of All Americans

Federal agencies should integrate hands-on technical training and apprenticeships into STEM education, open scientific careers to skilled craftspeople and practitioners, build dense regional innovation clusters that link research with advanced manufacturing, and ensure that the economic returns of discovery reach every region and community in the country.

title: Students' protest: Could breakthrough with Sonam Wangchuk help govt tackle crisis?
full_text:
Sonam Wangchuk when he broke his hunger strike

NEW DELHI: Government is keeping its fingers crossed after its successful attempt to persuade activist Sonam Wangchuk - whose wide recognition helped expand the reach of Cockroach Janta Party's protest into uncomfortable territory for BJP - to break his hunger strike. CJP's assertion, though, to continue and even escalate the agitation if its demand for education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation is not met has muddied the waters, but govt feels the successful engagement with the Ladakh activist coupled with measures taken by it will help counter the allegation that govt has not been sensitive to students' concerns and resonate with those not affiliated with AAP, the Left and other opponents and their student outfits. The breakthrough with Wangchuk became possible because of deft footwork, including behind-the-scenes moves by home minister Amit Shah, that saw ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh overcoming the activist and bringing in local netas of Ladakh. Wangchuk's fears about violence and the risk of protests being overtaken - something that he articulated in the video-graphed conversation with the ministers - were helpful. Official circles are hopeful that Wangchuk's appeal for peaceful protests and against any form of violence, besides govt's positive response to his demand for not registering criminal cases against peaceful protestors and suitable compensation to families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide, will have a positive impact and may also help isolate "genuine" students from activists motivated by a dizzying array of motives - from partisan political considerations and gender fluidity to angst over Brahmanical patriarchy and Manuvad and Hindutva dominance. Unlike Abhijeet Dipke-led CJP, Wangchuk has not insisted on Pradhan's resignation. Considering it as the hook that connected that segment of youth with the protest who are not overtly political and might have been even otherwise sympathetic to some of the causes of the party, Wangchuk nuancing his pitch for accountability for paper leaks and expanding it beyond the individual to the ministry should help a govt pitted against a determined and competitive push for the minister's scalp. PM Modi was quick on X to wish the Ladakh activist - who was detained under NSA last year for his alleged role in violent protest in the UT - and that he regains the weight he lost in the fast. CJP could not have been pleased with the turn of events, but it was careful not to express its annoyance. Dipke lauded Wangchuk's "extraordinary courage" but left no doubt that he would carry on with his protest until Pradhan was sacked. The rift was evident after Wangchuk's wife Gitanjali Angmo wrote on X, "Before you rush to criticise Wangchuk, first pause to earn the ethos of fasting for 26 days for a cause larger than yourself. He lies in the ICU today, having lost 11 kg, including muscle mass, because he chose sacrifice over comfort... The least we can offer him is a day of compassion before burdening him with our own expectations and political calculations. Not everyone is qualified to judge a life of selfless service. One must first earn the moral stature to do so. Please. Have a heart." Also read: CJP-Centre 3rd round of talks today; PM Modi, Wangchuk release late night video - top developments BJP's Amit Malviya was quick to take a jibe at Dipke, saying there is now little justification for "his gang" to continue the protest and alleged their objective no longer appears to address students' concerns but to manufacture a political victory by insisting on Pradhan's resignation. It was Wangchuk's forcible removal, although with court authorisation from the protest site on July 18 that imparted the first real burst of agitational energy into the campaign, before the protestors' march to Parliament and police's alleged heavy-handedness turned it into a national headline. title: Should the UK capital’s higher ed institutions be ‘Londonmaxxing’?
summary:
The Mayor of London has teamed up with London's institutions to make the case that the city is the higher education capital of the world. But what more can the city do to strengthen its case?

The post Should the UK capital’s higher ed institutions be ‘Londonmaxxing’? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Last week, Sadiq Khan joined forces with the capital’s universities, conservatoires, specialist institutions and research centres to make the case for London as the higher education capital of the world.

The campaign kicked off with an event at University College London to launch a new publication from London Higher, the voice of the capital’s higher education sector, which highlights the ways in which London combines scale, diversity and excellence of higher education unmatched among its global peers.

Speaking at the event, Tory Peer and chair of the APPG for London, Lord Kulveer Ranger, pointed out that London offers “world class” experiences in many areas that “we don’t shine a light on”.

If London institutions do not “do Londonmaxxing”, he suggested, other prominent cities around the world will continue to highlight all that they have to offer – potentially at the UK capital’s expense.

“[Other cities] champion what they have, and it’s our job to champion what we have, especially when it’s so good,” he said.

Meanwhile, future phases of the campaign will examine international student competitiveness, the sector’s contribution to economic growth and the policy conditions needed to support world-leading industries including life sciences and the creative economy.

The capital is home to more students and higher education institutions than international competitors like New York City, Boston and Singapore, while its universities generate economic activity, research breakthroughs and skilled graduates that support communities and industries around the UK and across the globe.

A strong higher education sector in London helps the whole country succeed. Every year our universities open doors for hundreds of thousands of students while supporting jobs, driving growth and strengthening the UK’s place on the world stage

Sadiq Khan, Mayor of London

In a foreword to the publication, Khan describes London’s higher education sector as a critical national asset, helping to drive growth, opportunity and international influence for the UK. The publication shows that:

London is the world’s leading higher education city by scale, diversity and global influence.

The capital combines a concentration of universities, specialist institutions and research centres found nowhere else on earth.

London’s higher education institutions contribute more to the UK economy than the Premier League and employ more people than Sainsbury’s nationwide.

The benefits generated by London’s higher education sector extend well beyond the capital through research collaboration, graduate talent, business creation and international investment.

Professor Shitij Kapur, chair of London Higher and vice-chancellor and president of King’s College London, called the capital’s higher education sector “one of the UK’s greatest strategic assets”.

“As a global city, London competes for talent, research and investment with the world’s leading centres of education and innovation. The strength of our higher education sector helps ensure the UK remains competitive, connected and influential on the world stage.

“But global leadership is never permanent. Cities around the world are investing heavily in higher education and innovation. If the UK wants to remain internationally competitive, we must continue to nurture the conditions that allow London’s universities and research institutions to thrive.”

Khan said: “London’s universities are among the very best in the world. They open doors for people from every background while leading the way in research and breakthroughs in areas such as life sciences and AI, where London’s leading the way.

“A strong higher education sector in London helps the whole country succeed. Every year our universities open doors for hundreds of thousands of students while supporting jobs, driving growth and strengthening the UK’s place on the world stage. That’s why higher education is such an important part of building a fairer and more prosperous London for everyone.”

title: An inclusive approach to an inclusive curriculum: transforming learning at the University of Northampton
summary: The post An inclusive approach to an inclusive curriculum: transforming learning at the University of Northampton appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
The University of Northampton shares a case study on a cross-university initiative to develop an Inclusive Curriculum Toolkit that is now embedded across learning, teaching and curriculum processes.

Creating an inclusive learning environment is a priority for higher education institutions seeking to improve student success, belonging and achievement. At the University of Northampton (UON), a cross-university initiative has turned this ambition into action through the development of an Inclusive Curriculum Toolkit that is now embedded across learning, teaching and curriculum processes.

Led by Professor Sian Davies-Vollum, Dr Faith Tucker and Associate Professor Dr Emma Whewell, alongside a team of academic and professional services colleagues, the project demonstrates how institutions can take a practical and sustainable approach to embedding inclusivity at the heart of the student experience.

Responding to staff and student needs

The project emerged from a Faculty of Education, Arts, Science and Technology development day focused on equality, diversity and inclusion in learning and teaching. Staff identified a clear need for accessible guidance that would help them translate inclusive principles into everyday practice.

This led to the creation of the Inclusive Curriculum Toolkit, a practical resource designed to support staff in developing curricula and learning experiences that meet the needs of increasingly diverse student populations.

The initiative aligns closely with the University’s commitment to inclusivity, widening participation and social impact. It was also developed to support the Learning, Teaching and Student Experience strategies while helping address challenges such as awarding gaps, student belonging and continuation.

Co-creating a toolkit for change

A key strength of the project was its collaborative approach. Over a two-year period, the toolkit was co-created with staff and students from across the institution, ensuring it reflected real experiences and practical needs.

The development process began with gathering insights through staff workshops, ‘Student Listening Rooms’ and student feedback activities. Those conversations informed a series of reflective prompt questions that encourage critical thinking about inclusivity within curriculum design and teaching practice.

The questions were reviewed by academic colleagues, professional services staff and external consultants to ensure they reflected both institutional priorities and sector best practice. The project then moved on to creating supportive multimedia resources before embedding the toolkit into university systems and processes.

A practical resource grounded in UDL

The toolkit is built on the principles of Universal Design for Learning (UDL), which promotes flexible approaches to teaching and assessment that support diverse learners from the outset.

Rather than viewing inclusion as an additional consideration, the toolkit positions it as a foundation of high-quality learning and teaching. It encourages staff to minimise barriers through curriculum design, reducing the need for retrospective adjustments.

The web-based resource acts as a central hub for inclusive learning and teaching. It combines existing guidance with newly developed content, including around 50 multimedia resources that explain not only what inclusive practice looks like, but also why it matters. Reflective questions, case studies and signposting help staff translate ideas into action.

Embedding inclusion across the institution

One of the project’s most significant achievements is the extent to which the toolkit has become embedded within University processes.

It is now used across curriculum development, curriculum review, academic induction and staff development. Staff are also required to reflect on their use of the toolkit as part of curriculum development, review and validation activities.

This level of integration helps ensure inclusivity becomes an established element of academic practice rather than a standalone initiative. The toolkit also supports key institutional priorities, including narrowing awarding gaps, improving students’ sense of belonging and enhancing continuation rates.

Lasting impact

The team’s work has already received significant recognition. In 2025, it received the University of Northampton’s People’s Award for Inclusivity Team of the Year.

The toolkit was officially launched at the University’s Learning and Teaching Conference in June 2026 and has now entered an evaluation phase. Short-term evaluation focuses on user experience and implementation, while longer-term monitoring will assess impact through curriculum documentation, engagement data, staff development activity and student outcomes.

Although developed specifically for the University of Northampton, the toolkit offers a valuable model for the wider higher education sector. Its success demonstrates the importance of collaboration, leadership support and embedding inclusion within institutional systems and processes.

title: Kinderschutz im Netz: Was die Politik plant, was Eltern tun können | c’t uplink
summary: Im Podcast besprechen wir, wie die Politik junge Menschen online schützen will und was Tiktok und Co. tun. Außerdem gibt‘s Tipps für Eltern und Jugendliche.
full_text:
Mobbing, Cybergrooming und suchtfördernde Algorithmen: Online kann gerade für Kinder und Jugendliche einiges schieflaufen. In dieser Folge vom c’t uplink geht es unter anderem darum, wie die Politik dem begegnet. Aktuell beschäftigt sich zum Beispiel die EU-Kommission mit dem Thema.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

c't uplink – der Podcast aus Nerdistan

Für die c’t-Ausgabe 16/2026 haben sich die c’t-Redakteure Jo Bager und Holger Bleich angesehen, wie sicher digitale Medien für Heranwachsende sind und welche Ansätze es gibt, um junge Menschen zu schützen. Im Podcast diskutieren sie mit c’t-Redakteurin Greta Friedrich darüber.

„In der Politik gibt es gerade einen Paradigmenwechsel, man guckt jetzt eher auf die digitalen Dienste selbst – Stichwort Social-Media-Verbot“, stellt Holger Bleich fest. Bisher hätten Dienste wie Tiktok, Instagram und Co. nämlich eher halbherzig versucht, die jungen Nutzer ihrer Plattformen zu schützen. „Es gibt zum Beispiel Whistleblower-Berichte, dass sie bei Meta genau gewusst haben, dass ihre Inhalte das Körperbild ihrer Nutzer, insbesondere von Mädchen, negativ beeinflussen. Und sie haben trotzdem nichts daran geändert“, erzählt Bleich.

Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe für Eltern & Kids

Da die Politik nicht von heute auf morgen Gesetze beschließt und durchsetzt, sollten auch Eltern, Lehrkräfte und Jugendliche selbst wissen, wie sie Gefahren im Netz begegnen. Denn unweigerlich kommen Kinder heute schon früh mit digitalen Medien in Kontakt. Die Eltern tippen auf dem Smartphone, der Fernseher läuft, Smart Speaker begleiten den Alltag zuhause. Spätestens ab der weiterführenden Schule gibt es oft ein eigenes Smartphone.

Jo Bager hat im c’t uplink einige Tipps für sie parat. „Für Eltern ist es ganz wichtig, ihrem Kind Interesse zu zeigen. title: Cultura: un’industria che vale 310 milioni. Traino del made in Italy
summary: A verona la Conferenza degli istituti italiani di cultura all’estero. Tajani: «Ambasciatori del Paese»
full_text:
L’Italia è un piccolo Paese: occupa appena lo 0,2% delle terre emerse, conta meno dell’1% della popolazione globale, eppure concentra nel suo territorio il 5% dei siti riconosciuti patrimonio dell’umanità dall’Unesco, genera il 3,1% dell’export globale e il 2,1% del prodotto interno lordo del Pianeta.

«Siamo una superpotenza culturale», osserva il ministro degli Affari esteri e della cooperazione internazionale, Antonio Tajani, intervenendo alla Conferenza delle direttrici e dei direttori degli Istituti italiani di cultura (IIC), che si è tenuta a Verona dal 20 al 23 luglio. Una rete di 88 soggetti in 63 Paesi, che realizzano annualmente oltre 5mila eventi promozionali, grazie a un investimento pubblico di circa 24 milioni l’anno. «La cultura è uno straordinario elemento di forza per promuovere la nostra identità e la nostra economia nel mondo e gli istituti di cultura sono ambasciatori di un’Italia che nella cultura è un gigante», ha detto Tajani.

La cultura è identità, è valori, è stile di vita. Ma è anche un motore di ricchezza e occupazione, come ha ricordato, intervenendo all’evento, Federico Silvestri, amministratore delegato del Gruppo il Sole 24 Ore, che nel 2023 ha iniziato a collaborare con il Maeci nel progetto Laboratorio Farnesina, trasformatosi nel 2026 in Laboratorio della Crescita. L’obiettivo è realizzare una mappatura delle iniziative e delle realtà italiane da sostenere e valorizzare all’estero attraverso la rete delle ambasciate, dei consolati e degli istituti italiani di cultura. Finora sono 11 le città italiane coinvolte, attraverso incontri uno a uno organizzati tra funzionari del Ministero e operatori locali della cultura, e tre i progetti realizzati. «Gli istituti italiani di cultura e il sistema della diplomazia culturale sono una infrastruttura strategica del Paese, che produce non solo conoscenza e sapere, ma anche competitività e crescita», ha detto Silvestri. I 170 miliardi di euro di export di prodotti belli e ben fatti, stimato da Confindustria, «ci ricordano che la reputazione culturale non è un elemento accessorio dell’economia, ma uno dei presupposti del suo valore», ha aggiunto, sottolineando che la cultura genera direttamente quasi 116 miliardi di euro di valore aggiunto e alimenta circa 49 miliardi in settori che della cultura beneficiano, dalla moda al design, dall’hospitality ai servizi.

Anche il ministro Tajani ha ricordato alcuni numeri che restituiscono l’importanza della cultura non solo dal punto di vista identitario, ma anche economico. «L’industria della cultura vale 310 miliardi, pari al 15,4% della ricchezza nazionale – ha detto Tajani, citando i dati contenuti nel Rapporto Io sono cultura di Fondazione Symbola, presentato la scorsa settimana – e dà lavoro a un milione e mezzo di persone, il 5,7% dell’occupazione italiana».

L’industria culturale comprende non solo i settori tradizionalmente intesi come tali, ma anche comparti produttivi che partecipano a pieno titolo a creare l’identità e lo stile di vita italiani. Lo ha precisato Matteo Zoppas, presidente dell’Agenzia Ice, osservando che «noi italiani siamo famosi nel mondo non solo per la nostra cultura artistica, ma anche per quella artigianale e industriale, trasversale a diversi settori, tra cui design, moda, cucina e vino, tecnologia e artigianato». Zoppas ha ricordato il lavoro di sinergia tra i 90 uffici Ice nel mondo e gli istituti italiani di cultura, sotto la regia del Maeci. «La cultura è ambasciatrice di dialogo e di pace, ma è anche diplomazia della crescita, a supporto dell’obiettivo del governo di raggiungere i 700 miliardi di euro di export nel 2027».

«We are a cultural superpower», observes the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Antonio Tajani, speaking at the Conference of directors of the Italian Institutes of Culture (IIC), which was held in Verona from 20 to 23 July. A network of 88 entities in 63 countries, which organize over 5 thousand promotional events annually, thanks to a public investment of around 24 million per year. «Culture is an extraordinary element of strength for promoting our identity and our economy in the world and cultural institutes are ambassadors of an Italy that is a giant in culture», said Tajani.

Culture is identity, it is values, it is lifestyle. But it is also an engine of wealth and employment, as recalled, speaking at the event, by Federico Silvestri, CEO of the Il Sole 24 Ore Group, who in 2023 began collaborating with Maeci in the Farnesina Laboratory project, which transformed into the Growth Laboratory in 2026. So far, 11 Italian cities have been involved, through one-to-one meetings organized between Ministry officials and local cultural operators, and three projects have been implemented. «The Italian cultural institutes and the cultural diplomacy system are a strategic infrastructure of the country, which produces not only knowledge and knowledge, but also competitiveness and growth», said Silvestri. Minister Tajani also recalled some numbers that show the importance of culture not only from an identity point of view, but also from an economic point of view. «The culture industry is worth 310 billion, equal to 15.4% of national wealth – said Tajani, citing the data contained in the Symbola Foundation's Io sono cultura report, presented last week – and provides work to one and a half million people, 5.7% of Italian employment».

The cultural industry includes not only the sectors traditionally understood as such, but also production sectors that fully participate in creating the Italian identity and lifestyle. This was specified by Matteo Zoppas, president of the Ice Agency, observing that «we Italians are famous in the world not only for our artistic culture, but also for our artisanal and industrial culture, which cuts across various sectors, including design, fashion, cuisine and wine, technology and craftsmanship». Zoppas recalled the synergy work between the 90 Ice offices in the world and the Italian cultural institutes, under the direction of Maeci. «Culture is an ambassador of dialogue and peace, but it is also growth diplomacy, in support of the government's objective of reaching 700 billion euros in exports in 2027».

title: La fine dell’ASN e il nuovo “semaforo”: la riforma Bernini tra burocrazia e vecchi vizi
summary: L’abolizione dell’ASN sostituisce il giudizio delle commissioni nazionali con un sistema quantitativo “a semaforo”, eliminando la valutazione qualitativa della ricerca. La riforma lascia però irrisolte le criticità dei concorsi locali, aumentando anzi il rischio di bandi profilati “su misura” per i candidati interni.  L’ASN finisce nel dimenticatoio dopo 15 lunghi anni. Significativa è la circostanza […]
full_text:
L’abolizione dell’ASN sostituisce il giudizio delle commissioni nazionali con un sistema quantitativo “a semaforo”, eliminando la valutazione qualitativa della ricerca. La riforma lascia però irrisolte le criticità dei concorsi locali, aumentando anzi il rischio di bandi profilati “su misura” per i candidati interni.

L’ASN finisce nel dimenticatoio dopo 15 lunghi anni. Significativa è la circostanza che a decretarne la morte sia la proposta di una Ministra (Bernini) appartenente al medesimo partito politico di chi la volle (Gelmini).

Sulla bontà, validità, efficacia e, soprattutto, equità dell’Abilitazione sono stati spesi fiumi d’inchiostro e questo mio intervento si limiterà a formulare alcune elementari considerazioni sul suo (distorto) funzionamento, sia dal punto di vista diacronico, sia dal punto di vista sincronico. Vi sono stati, infatti, Settori Concorsuali nel quali abilitarsi era quasi impossibile, in particolare se si finiva nel tritacarne delle vendette trasversali fra baroni, nel mentre in altri Settori si abilitavano praticamente tutti. Ve ne sono stati alcuni nei quali l’agognato risultato giungeva dopo un lungo contenzioso giurisdizionale (anche questo con alterne vicende) e altri, invece, i cui risultati apparivano già decisi prim’ancora delle riunioni d’insediamento.

L’ASN doveva essere, almeno nelle intenzioni del legislatore e di chi fra noi l’ha criticata, ma accettata, una mera “constatazione” del possesso di requisiti e pubblicazioni tali da consentire di partecipare alla selezione vera, rappresentata dal concorso locale e non una forca caudina talvolta insuperabile per alcuni e un’autostrada in discesa per altri.

Ma essa ha avuto, come pure è stato molto opportunamente notato taluni commentatori anche su questo sito, conseguenze importanti che hanno “riorganizzato”, in peggio, l’intero comparto della ricerca universitaria, fatto ora solo di prodotti della ricerca, convegni e seminari, riviste di classe A, indici bibliometrici, pubblicazioni a pagamento, crescita esponenziale delle citazioni, ma anche, più in generale, di articoli e saggi. Mi è personalmente capitato di scorrere la produzione scientifica di un collega di area giuridica che in biennio ha dichiarato di aver pubblicato 30 contributi, di cui 20 in classe A, circostanza che francamente nessuna persona di buon senso può considerare come ragionevole e corretta.

Tutto questo accadrà di nuovo, purtroppo, perché l’ASN è stata soppiantata da una procedura “a semaforo”, nella quale gli studiosi presenteranno una dichiarazione sostitutiva di certificazione del possesso di requisiti che verranno individuati con apposito Decreto ministeriale. Tutto si fonderà, conseguentemente, sotto il profilo “quantitativo” e nessuna Commissione nazionale potrà giudicare la bontà e la qualità della produzione scientifica, passando ai raggi x ogni singola pubblicazione. Da questo punto di vista se si voleva eliminare la discrezionalità (buona o cattiva) delle Commissioni Nazionali di Abilitazione, l’obiettivo mi parrebbe esser stato pienamente raggiunto.

Tutti i candidati, quindi, in possesso della vecchia ASN o dei nuovi requisiti sono legittimati, di conseguenza, a partecipare alle selezioni locali, procedura su cui la nuova legge mi sembrerebbe essere intervenuta in maniera talvolta piuttosto timida, talaltra introducendo veri e propri buchi neri in grado di minare la trasparenza delle procedure medesime.

Il capitolo sulla composizione delle commissioni giudicatrici locali viene affrontato e modificato (si passa da 3 a 5 commissari, sorteggiati su base nazionale da liste di docenti dichiaratisi disponibili e in possesso di precisi requisiti), ma si è evitato di incidere in maniera più pregnante sulle loro dinamiche, quasi da far apparire l’estensore della norma come un soggetto che non ha mai frequentato un ufficio universitario. Perché non si è reintrodotto (come un tempo) il divieto di far parte delle Commissioni nei primi tre anni di servizio, in modo da evitare che i neofiti possano immediatamente selezionare i loro colleghi, evidentemente sdebitandosi? Perché è stata introdotta l’incandidabilità solo a seguito di condanne passate in giudicato (come è noto abrogato l’abuso d’ufficio, salvo rari casi, i concorsi universitari non temono i procedimenti penali)? Perché non sono stati introdotti meccanismi sanzionatori nei confronti di quelle Commissioni di concorso i cui esiti sono stati rovesciati dalla giurisprudenza amministrativa?

Resta, infine, l’infelice possibile interpretazione di quella parte della nuova legge che consentirebbe di introdurre una profilazione puntuale e precisa nel bando (un tempo si diceva della possibilità di “cucire addosso” al candidato il bando per consentirgli di vincere, prima ancora di cominciare, la selezione). Qui il legislatore ha commesso un grave e temo irrimediabile errore che è destinato a rendere praticamente inutile tutta la procedura: un tempo non era consentito e talvolta il giudice sanzionava gli Atenei, oggi tale circostanza entra dalla porta principale ed è destinata a far discutere. Su questo punto temo che il rimedio sia stato peggiore del male.
